clue.text: For example, Perrier Award certain to be less independent when restructured

indicators.note: less means minus, so a letter is taken away from the material
something restructured has had its parts rebuilt in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
I is the standard abbreviation for independent

explanation.surface: A comedy prize sponsored by a mineral-water brand is about to lose its independence in a corporate shake-up.
explanation.walkthrough: The Perrier Award was the famous Edinburgh Fringe comedy prize, so 'Award' looks attached to it; in fact Perrier is the definition and 'Award certain to be' is the material, minus one I.
explanation.definitionFit: Perrier is a French brand of sparkling mineral water, an example of fizzy bottled drinks.

clue.text: Mischievously inscribe an item with tip from Tommy Cooper maybe

indicators.note: acting mischievously means making trouble, so the letters are messed about
the tip of a word is its very first letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letter of Tommy

explanation.surface: Someone playfully engraves a keepsake for the fez-wearing comic Tommy Cooper.
explanation.walkthrough: Tommy Cooper was a much-loved British comedy magician, so 'Tommy Cooper' reads as one name; split it, and Cooper alone is Yvette Cooper, a senior Labour politician.
explanation.definitionFit: Yvette Cooper has held senior government posts such as Home Secretary, so she is an example of a member of the cabinet.

clue.text: They make good couple on TV show – breaking short series up

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece sitting on another means it comes first, directly above
to break into something is to force a way inside it
in a down clue, going up means reading from the bottom to the top

blocks.note: ser. is the short form of series
a couple is a pair
ER is the American hospital drama series

explanation.surface: A celebrity couple are a good match on a TV show, until a brief run of episodes gets in the way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'They make good couple' reads as a compliment on a pairing, but only 'They make good' defines: to make good is to mend. ER is the American hospital drama.
explanation.definitionFit: To make good is an idiom for to repair or restore something, and those who do it are menders.

clue.text: Cricket ground – somewhere to go round in retirement

indicators.note: to retire is to withdraw or go back, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a lav, short for lavatory, is where you go when you need to go
a round shape is the letter O

explanation.surface: A cricket ground is pictured as a pleasant place for a pensioner to stroll around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somewhere to go' is the lavatory, a common euphemism. THE OVAL is a London Test cricket ground, home of Surrey.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oval in Kennington, south London, is a famous venue for international Test matches.

clue.text: Having beer with Charlie - Guinness?

blocks.note: ale is a kind of beer
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone drinks a beer with their friend Charlie and asks if it is a pint of Guinness.
explanation.walkthrough: Guinness is the Irish stout, so it sits naturally beside beer; here it is the actor's surname, with the question mark flagging an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Alec Guinness was the British actor famed for Obi-Wan Kenobi and Ealing comedies, so his first name answers.

clue.text: Mounting madness after old woman abandoned ship - escaping death

indicators.note: what is abandoned is left behind, so those letters drop out
something escaping gets away, so it is no longer there
in a down clue, mounting means climbing, so the letters read upwards

blocks.note: taken as written
one's old woman is slang for one's mother, ma
SS stands for steamship

explanation.surface: Panic rises aboard after an elderly woman abandons ship, narrowly cheating death.
explanation.walkthrough: The word itself is the material: take the mother and the steamship out of 'madness' and what is left, read upwards, is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The end of a life is its finish, so end is a common euphemism for dying.

clue.text: Club with spirits and cider?

blocks.note: a wood is a golf club with a large head
pecker is British slang for courage, as in 'keep your pecker up'

explanation.surface: A drinking club serves hard liquor alongside its apple drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirits' suggests alcohol beside 'cider', but it means morale. The question mark warns that 'cider' is defined by a brand name.
explanation.definitionFit: Woodpecker is a long-established British brand of sweet cider made by Bulmers, so the bird's name labels the drink.

clue.text: Misfit team manager is one using English left back

indicators.note: going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the letters read the other way

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
port is the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: A hapless football manager plays an Englishman at left back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left back' is a football position, but here 'left' is the nautical word and 'back' turns the letters round.
explanation.definitionFit: The scruffy coach of a team of misfits who come good is a familiar storytelling device in sports films.

clue.text: Discophile making my day following deal with binman

indicators.note: to make one thing into another is to turn it into something different, swapping one part for another

blocks.note: a discophile collects gramophone records
Cor! is a British exclamation of surprise, like My!
D is the abbreviation for day
f. is the abbreviation for following, as in page references
to use something is to deal with or handle it

explanation.surface: A vinyl enthusiast is thrilled at striking a bargain with the dustman over a box of discs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make my day' is a catchphrase, but here COR (my) plus D (day) is swapped out of the discophile and F plus USE put in. A binman is a British rubbish collector.
explanation.definitionFit: A binman empties household bins, and refuse collector is the formal job title for that work.

clue.text: Flyer told to pay for uniform?

indicators.note: something told is spoken to someone, so it is the sound that counts

blocks.note: to pay for something is to buy it
uniform in the sense of unvaried, featureless

explanation.surface: A pilot is ordered to pay for their own uniform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uniform' looks like a noun, the pilot's kit, but it is the adjective meaning plain and unvaried.
explanation.definitionFit: A biplane is an aircraft with two pairs of wings, and anything that flies can be called a flyer.

clue.text: Delivery of sink cancelled

blocks.note: to sink is to drop down
an event that is cancelled is off

explanation.surface: A plumber's merchant has called off the delivery of a kitchen sink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sink' looks like the thing being delivered, a basin; it is the verb meaning fall.
explanation.definitionFit: A drop-off is the act of leaving goods or a person at a destination, which is a delivery.

clue.text: Artificial Intelligence – oddly local children accepted digital refinement tool

indicators.note: oddly here means taking only the odd-numbered letters, the first, third and fifth
whatever is accepted is taken in, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: nippers is British slang for small children
AI is the standard abbreviation
the odd letters of local

explanation.surface: Local schoolchildren take to an AI gadget for touching up digital photos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digital refinement tool' sounds like photo-editing software; digits here are fingers and toes.
explanation.definitionFit: Clippers trim and tidy the nails on fingers and toes, which are digits, so they refine them.

clue.text: See 11
Flush loo – handle occasionally stays down (have wiped)

indicators.note: only some letters stay, now and then, so every other one is kept
what is wiped is erased, so those letters are rubbed out

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters
taken as written
to have something is to own it

explanation.surface: A toilet's flush handle keeps sticking down, and the bracket adds that the user has already wiped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flush' looks like the toilet verb but is the adjective for well off. The bracketed 'have wiped' is wordplay too: own, meaning have, is wiped from the word down.
explanation.definitionFit: Flush is informal for having plenty of money, and loaded is slang for being very rich.

clue.text: Instrument used to ride cycles through gunge?

indicators.note: a cycle goes round, so the word's last letter comes round to the front
going through something means passing inside it

blocks.note: 'I used to' can be put as 'I did', in the habitual past
goo is sticky gunge
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether an instrument was once used to ride bikes through mud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycles' sounds like bicycles, but it moves the last letter of the word to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: The didgeridoo is a long wooden wind instrument of Aboriginal Australians, blown to make a droning sound.

clue.text: Some remember that collar

indicators.note: some of something is only a part, so the letters lie inside the phrase

blocks.note: found across the two words

explanation.surface: A reminder to recall a particular collar.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts in the middle of 'remember' and ends inside 'that'.
explanation.definitionFit: A bertha is a deep, wide collar on a low-necked dress, often of lace, popular in Victorian fashion.

clue.text: Mostly they enjoy similar things

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: the word without its last letter
to enjoy something is to like it

explanation.surface: A general remark that people mostly like the same things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mostly' reads as 'usually', but it trims the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: In phrases such as 'and the like', the expression stands for other items of the same kind.

clue.text: Monk, say, when jerk joins church

indicators.note: joining things puts them side by side, one after another

blocks.note: as can mean when, as in 'as I left'
CE is the Church of England
a tic is an involuntary jerk

explanation.surface: A monk is compared to someone who, after a spasm, signs up to a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jerk' looks like an insult for a person; it is a twitch.
explanation.definitionFit: A monk renounces comfort and pleasure for religious reasons, which is an example of someone living austerely.

clue.text: Working accordingly during test of hairdressing

indicators.note: something happening during an event sits within its span

blocks.note: a trial is a test
a machine that is working is on
so means accordingly, therefore

explanation.surface: A trainee hairdresser is being assessed in a practical exam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of hairdressing' is an adjective phrase, matching the answer's part of speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonsorial comes from the Latin for barber and describes anything relating to barbers or cutting hair.

clue.text: Make out with Diane regularly seeking penetration

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

blocks.note: the second and fourth letters
to make out something in the distance is to sight it

explanation.surface: A racy picture of someone getting amorous with Diane on a regular basis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make out' suggests kissing, but means to see; 'penetration' is the mental kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Penetration can mean keen understanding, the ability to see deeply into a problem, which is perceptiveness.

clue.text: Everlasting Love – hit single over in America – Carl finally makes it

indicators.note: finally points to the end of each word, so only closing letters are kept

blocks.clueFragment: Love – hit single over in America – Carl
blocks.note: the final letter of each of the seven words

explanation.surface: A pop note: the song Everlasting Love was a hit stateside, and Carl Carlton is the singer who finally made it with it.
explanation.walkthrough: The italic title tempts you to treat 'Everlasting Love' as one unit; only 'Everlasting' defines, and 'Love' begins the run of word endings. Carl Carlton's 1974 cover was the American hit.
explanation.definitionFit: Something everlasting never ends, and eternal is the standard synonym for lasting for ever without stopping.

clue.text: Ace encore music playing – without American cornet

indicators.note: without means lacking, so those letters are taken away
the letters are played about with, like notes rearranged in a new tune

blocks.note: taken as written
US stands for the United States

explanation.surface: A band plays a superb encore, but without the American cornet player.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cornet' sits among musical words as a brass instrument, but it is the British word for a wafer cone.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a cornet is the conical wafer holding a scoop of ice cream, the same thing Americans call a cone.

clue.text: Key material drawn by Hergé conclusively?

indicators.note: conclusively points to the conclusion, so only the final letter is taken

blocks.note: the final letter of the Tintin artist's name
a drawn face is thin and gaunt

explanation.surface: A crucial clue sketched by the creator of Tintin, as in a comic-strip mystery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawn' suggests a cartoonist's pen, given Hergé, but means haggard.
explanation.definitionFit: The black keys of a piano were traditionally made of ebony, a dense dark hardwood, so it is key material.

clue.text: See 21
Daughter remains in touch

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for daughter
ash is what remains after burning, including cremated remains

explanation.surface: An estranged daughter still keeps in contact.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In touch' reads as a phrase about contact; 'in' only joins, and 'touch' means a small amount.
explanation.definitionFit: A touch of salt and a dash of salt both mean a small added quantity of something.

clue.text: Put favourable slant on offence involving parking

indicators.note: to involve something is to include it, holding it within

blocks.note: a sin is a moral offence
P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking

explanation.surface: Someone tries to talk their way out of a parking ticket by putting a positive gloss on it.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a verb phrase, matching spin as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To spin a story is the political idiom for presenting news in a way that flatters your own side.

clue.text: Possibly radish on the counter as requested

indicators.note: counter means against or opposite, so the letters run the opposite way

blocks.note: a radish is an example of a red root vegetable

explanation.surface: A greengrocer puts a radish on the shop counter for a customer who asked for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the counter' paints a shop scene, but counter here means going against the normal direction.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods made to order are produced to a customer's specification, just as they asked.

clue.text: Staff enter no bid, according to terms

indicators.note: a terminus is an end point, so terms are the closing letters of each word

blocks.note: the final letter of each of the three words

explanation.surface: Employees are told to make no offer, as their contract stipulates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff' reads as employees, but it is a stick, and 'terms' are word endings, not contract conditions.
explanation.definitionFit: A staff is a long stick or pole, such as a shepherd's crook or a bishop's crozier.

clue.text: Select a quiet property

blocks.note: taken as written
p, piano, is the musical direction for quiet
a point is a characteristic, as in 'his strong points'

explanation.surface: An estate agent is asked to pick out a peaceful house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Property' suggests real estate but means a quality or feature.
explanation.definitionFit: To appoint someone is to choose or name them for a job or role.

clue.text: Run article Henry McDonald edited for writer

indicators.note: editing a text changes it about, so the letters are reworked

blocks.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run
a is the indefinite article
taken as written

explanation.surface: A newspaper runs a piece that an editor called Henry McDonald has subbed for a contributor.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry McDonald reads as a real journalist's byline; his whole name is raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: Raymond Chandler was the American author of hardboiled detective novels such as The Big Sleep, featuring Philip Marlowe.
